nodes.label: PersistenceQuery
nodes.rationale: The read-side API over the journal in two flavours: current* resolves once with a materialized array, events* is a live AsyncIterable that polls until the consumer stops. The interface is identical across implementations — construct the one for your backend and pass it the journal instance, not a connection string.

nodes.label: InMemoryQuery
nodes.rationale: The reference implementation, not the in-memory-only one: it works against ANY Journal, so a backend without its own query class can still run projections. What is lost is the index, and only on the by-tag methods — currentEventsByTag lists every persistence id, replays each from sequence 1 and filters in process, per call. Correct at any volume, fast only at small ones, and nothing warns you.

nodes.label: RelationalQuery
nodes.rationale: The dialect-neutral base for any RelationalJournal; PostgresQuery and MariaDbQuery are named subclasses of it.

nodes.label: Offset
nodes.rationale: A compound (timestamp, persistenceId, sequenceNr) — timestamp orders the stream, persistenceId breaks ties, sequenceNr breaks them within one entity. So events from different entities interleave by timestamp while events from one entity keep their original sequence. Persist the offset returned with each event and resume from it.

nodes.label: TagFilter
nodes.rationale: any / all / a combination of both; a bare tag string is equivalent to { all: [tag] }.

nodes.label: currentPersistenceIdsPaginated
nodes.rationale: Pages the id list so peak memory is one page rather than the whole set — currentPersistenceIds is the only method with no bound on what it allocates. The cursor is a persistence id, not an opaque token, so a partial walk resumes by passing the last id handled; ids come back in the backend's ascending order and the cursor is compared in that same order, so which collation it is never matters to the consumer.

nodes.label: allPersistenceIds
nodes.rationale: The fan-out primitive — every id ever seen, then each new one as it appears. Delivery is once per stream, not once per journal, so a consumer that must not act twice across a restart needs its own checkpoint. The stream holds an in-process set of everything it emitted; a cheaper high-water mark would be wrong because ids are not created in sorted order, so an id sorting below the mark would never be emitted at all.

nodes.label: LiveQueryOptions polling
nodes.rationale: Live streams poll at pollIntervalMs (default 1000). Light at idle, but under heavy write load polling piles up if the read side is slower than the write side. Sub-poll-interval delivery needs the push-based query.

nodes.label: A compacted event leaves the tag index too
nodes.rationale: delete is specified against the read side as well: once a prefix is compacted, currentEventsByTag stops returning it. Backends whose index sits on the event record get that for free; those with a separate structure delete from it in the same call and BEFORE the events, so a crash mid-delete cannot strand rows whose keys are no longer reconstructible. Worth knowing when writing your own journal — read and highestSeq look perfectly correct while a forgotten index keeps serving deleted events.

nodes.label: Id pagination is pushed down only where a sorted key exists
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY … LIMIT on the SQL backends, a clustering-column range on Cassandra's all_persistence_ids table. MongoDB and DynamoDB have no such index — distinct has no cursor and a Scan has no order across partition keys — so there the page is cut in-process and pagination buys ergonomics, not I/O.
